questions.title: How Database Indexes Work
questions.question: How do database indexes work and how do you decide which columns to index?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **B-tree index: balanced tree, O(log n) lookup — default index type**
- **Index speeds reads but slows writes (insert/update/delete must update index)**
- **Index columns that appear in WHERE, JOIN ON, ORDER BY**
- **Composite index: column order matters — leftmost prefix rule**
- **Covering index: includes all columns the query needs — avoids table lookup**
- **Don't over-index: each index costs write performance and storage**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
An index is a separate data structure (B-tree by default in most RDBMS) that allows the database to locate rows without scanning the entire table. Without an index, every query does a full table scan — O(n). With a B-tree index, lookup is O(log n). The trade-off: indexes consume disk space and must be updated on every write.

You should index columns that appear frequently in WHERE clauses, JOIN conditions, or ORDER BY clauses on large tables. For composite indexes (multiple columns), the order matters — the database can use the index for queries on the leftmost columns, but not if you skip the first column.

The covering index technique is powerful for read-heavy queries: if you include all the columns a query needs directly in the index, the database never touches the main table — it answers the query entirely from the index.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## B-Tree Index Structure

```
Table: orders (10 million rows)
Columns: id, user_id, status, total, created_at

WITHOUT index on user_id:
  SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42
  → Full table scan: read all 10M rows → slow (seconds)

WITH B-tree index on user_id:
  → B-tree lookup: O(log 10M) ≈ 23 comparisons → fast (milliseconds)

B-Tree structure:
         [500]
        /     \
    [250]      [750]
   /     \    /     \
[100] [375] [600] [900]

Each node stores key values and pointers to child nodes or data rows.
Leaf nodes are linked → range scans are efficient.
```

## When to Index

```sql
-- INDEX THIS: High-cardinality columns in WHERE/JOIN
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
-- Cardinality: 1M unique users → index very selective → big win

-- DON'T INDEX THIS: Low-cardinality columns
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status ON orders(status);
-- Cardinality: only 5 statuses (PENDING, CONFIRMED, etc.)
-- Index returns 20% of rows → full scan might be faster
-- Exception: combine with other high-cardinality columns in composite index

-- INDEX ORDER BY columns on large result sets:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at);
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
-- Without index: sort 10M rows → with index: read 20 from sorted structure

-- INDEX JOIN columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id ON order_items(order_id);
SELECT o.id, i.product_id FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON o.id = i.order_id;
-- order_id is FK — always index FK columns!
```

## Composite Index — Column Order Matters

```sql
-- Composite index: (user_id, status, created_at)
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_status_created ON orders(user_id, status, created_at);

-- Leftmost prefix rule:
-- ✓ Can use index:
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;                          -- Prefix: user_id
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING';  -- Prefix: user_id, status
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42 AND status = 'PENDING'   -- All three
    AND created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- ✗ Cannot use index (skips user_id):
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING';         -- No user_id → can't use
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'; -- No user_id → can't use

-- Optimize column order: most selective first + matches common query patterns
-- If you always filter by user_id → put it first
-- If most queries filter by user_id + status → (user_id, status) together
```

## Covering Index

```sql
-- Query: get order id and total for a user
SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;

-- Regular index on user_id:
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → get row pointers
-- 2. Fetch actual rows from table → read 'id' and 'total'
-- (Two I/O operations: index + table)

-- Covering index includes all needed columns:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_covering ON orders(user_id, id, total);
-- 1. Look up user_id = 42 in index → directly read id and total from index
-- (One I/O operation: index only — no table access)

-- PostgreSQL: EXPLAIN shows "Index Only Scan" for covering indexes
-- MySQL: EXPLAIN shows "Using index" in Extra column

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE example:
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT id, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Shows: Index Only Scan using idx_orders_user_covering
--        Rows: 15, actual time: 0.05ms (vs 450ms without index)
```

## Index Impact on Writes

```
Table with 5 indexes:
  idx_user_id
  idx_status
  idx_created_at
  idx_user_status_created (composite)
  idx_user_covering

INSERT into orders:
  → Write row to table
  → Update ALL 5 indexes
  → 6× write operations (1 table + 5 indexes)

UPDATE orders SET status = 'CONFIRMED' WHERE id = 1:
  → Update table row
  → Update idx_status (value changed)
  → Update idx_user_status_created (status changed)
  → 3× write operations

Conclusion:
  - High-write tables: minimize indexes
  - Read-heavy tables: more indexes acceptable
  - Remove unused indexes: query pg_stat_user_indexes / sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats
```

## Production Reality

Always add indexes on foreign key columns (MySQL doesn't do this automatically). Use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` to verify index usage — sometimes the query planner skips the index if it estimates a full scan is faster (usually correct for small tables or low-cardinality filters). Periodically audit unused indexes using your database's index usage statistics. In PostgreSQL, `pg_stat_user_indexes` shows scan counts — drop indexes with zero scans (in production, over a representative period).
